Everything in this course so far produced evidence. This unit turns evidence into a document other people can judge: figures drawn at their final size in code, tables whose digits mean what they appear to mean, a Methods section detailed enough for a stranger to reproduce the result, the reporting checklists reviewers in our fields actually apply, and an honest account of how the text and the code were written — including the part written with a language model. The unit is deliberately mechanical: almost every object in a paper can be generated from the analysis itself, and the ones that are generated are the ones that stay correct when a number changes.

Resumen en español

Esta unidad trata la última etapa de un proyecto: convertir resultados en un manuscrito defendible. Se construyen figuras de calidad de publicación íntegramente con código (tamaño en centímetros, resolución, exportación a PDF y SVG con tipografías incrustadas, hojas de estilo con rcParams, paneles con letras, comprobaciones de daltonismo y de escala de grises) y se rehace una figura exploratoria del curso como figura de dos paneles. Se diseñan tablas con cifras significativas coherentes con su incertidumbre y suplementos legibles por máquina con su diccionario de datos. Se redacta la sección de Métodos del modelo de ROCK1 a partir de la procedencia capturada por el propio cuaderno, y se completan las listas de verificación que exige la literatura del grupo: principios de validación de la OCDE y formato QMRF, TRIPOD+AI, MIAME/MINSEQE y las buenas prácticas de LiveCoMS. Finalmente se tratan las declaraciones de disponibilidad de datos y código, las licencias, la estructura narrativa del artículo y el uso declarado y verificado de modelos de lenguaje, con una comprobación automática de la integridad de las referencias contra Crossref.

Learning objectives

  • Produce publication-quality figures programmatically (vector formats, physical sizes, fonts, multi-panel layouts, colour) that pass journal requirements without manual editing.
  • Design tables and supplementary material that a reader can reuse, and write Methods that allow replication (software versions, parameters, seeds, data sources).
  • Apply the reporting checklists relevant to the laboratory — OECD principles and QMRF, TRIPOD+AI for clinical prediction, MIAME/MINSEQE for omics, LiveCoMS best practices for simulation — and the journal's data and code policies.
  • Use large language models in writing and coding ethically and transparently, and detect the failure mode that matters most: fabricated or mismatched references.
  • Avoid the common writing pitfalls of computational papers: over-claiming, metric cherry-picking, uncredited data and figures that mislead.

How to read this notebook

Run every cell from top to bottom; every number quoted in the prose is printed by the cell above or below it. In Colab run !pip install rdkit tabulate once before the setup cell. One cell in Section 13 queries the public Crossref API; it is wrapped in try/except and falls back to a frozen copy of the responses, and the notebook prints which path it took. Everything else runs offline from ../data/. The model whose results are reported throughout is refitted here in under a minute, so the Methods section and the checklists describe a model that exists rather than one quoted from elsewhere.

# Setup. In Google Colab run once:  !pip install rdkit tabulate
from pathlib import Path
import urllib.request, json, hashlib, platform, textwrap, math, warnings, sys, tempfile, shutil, re, io
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import sklearn, rdkit, scipy
from rdkit import Chem, RDLogger
from rdkit.Chem import rdFingerprintGenerator
RDLogger.DisableLog("rdApp.*")
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

SEED = 0
np.random.seed(SEED)
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "font.size": 9, "axes.titlesize": 10,
                     "axes.titleweight": "bold", "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})

REPO = "DanielBustosG/DanielBustosG.github.io"   # GitHub repository hosting this course (set once in common/config.json and here)
DATA_URL = f"https://raw.githubusercontent.com/{REPO}/main/DataScience/data/"
def data_path(name):
    '''Local ../data/<name> when the notebook runs from its course folder; otherwise (Colab) download once.'''
    local = Path("..") / "data" / name
    if local.exists():
        return local
    dest = Path("data") / name
    if not dest.exists():
        dest.parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(DATA_URL + name, dest)
    return dest
def load_data(name, **kw):
    return pd.read_csv(data_path(name), **kw)

WORK = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="u23_"))   # scratch folder for exported figures, tables and supplements
print("python", platform.python_version(), "| numpy", np.__version__, "| pandas", pd.__version__,
      "| scipy", scipy.__version__, "| matplotlib", matplotlib.__version__,
      "| scikit-learn", sklearn.__version__, "| rdkit", rdkit.__version__)
print("scratch folder:", WORK)

1. What the last mile is for

A paper is not a report of what you did; it is an argument that a specific claim is supported by specific evidence, written so that a sceptical reader can check it. Three audiences read it, in this order: an editor deciding whether to send it out, two or three referees deciding whether the evidence supports the claim, and — if it survives — the student in another laboratory who wants to reuse the method two years later. Each of them reads different parts. The editor reads the title, the abstract and the figures. The referee reads the figures, then the Methods, then the parts of the Results that the figures made them suspicious about. The reuser reads the Methods and the data-availability statement and nothing else.

This ordering explains the advice the laboratory repeats to every student: assemble the figures first, then write the story around them[9]. A figure that cannot be explained in two sentences is usually an analysis that has not finished, and writing the captions before the Results forces every claim to point at visible evidence.

The second reason the last mile deserves a whole unit is that almost all of it can be computed. A figure drawn by code can be redrawn when the model is refitted; a figure assembled by hand in a drawing program cannot, and so it quietly stops matching the numbers. A Methods paragraph generated from the environment that ran the analysis cannot claim the wrong version of scikit-learn. Reproducibility failures in computational papers are overwhelmingly bookkeeping failures, not conceptual ones[14][20][33], and bookkeeping is what a notebook is good at.

Domain context — where the group publishes, and what its referees check

The laboratory works at the intersection of computational chemistry, bioinformatics and machine learning for drug discovery, and publishes in journals that are Q1 or Q2 and charge no article-processing fee to the author. In practice that means outlets of the Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling, Journal of Cheminformatics, Bioinformatics, Briefings in Bioinformatics, Molecules, International Journal of Molecular Sciences, Pharmaceuticals and Frontiers type. A QSAR paper (quantitative structure–activity relationship: a model that predicts a biological activity from the chemical structure of a compound) submitted to such a journal is checked by referees for a short list of things, almost always the same list: is the data set described well enough to be rebuilt, including the target, the assay types and the curation; is the validation external rather than only internal; is the applicability domain — the region of chemical space where the model may be trusted — defined; are the performance metrics reported on the split that matches the claim; are the compounds and the code available. These are not matters of taste. They are the five OECD principles for the validation of (Q)SAR models[12][13], and Section 10 fills them in for the model this notebook fits.

A thesis and a paper contain the same evidence in different documents. The thesis shows the path, including the failed featurisation and the split that leaked; the paper shows the destination and the evidence that it is the right one. The discipline this unit teaches is to decide, for every object you produce, whether it belongs in the paper, in the supplement, in the repository or in the thesis only.

# The data and the model whose results this unit reports. One row per standardised compound.
df = load_data("rock1_chembl_curated.csv")
exact = df.loc[~df["censored"]].reset_index(drop=True)      # regression target defined only for exact values
DESC = ["MolWt", "MolLogP", "TPSA", "HBD", "HBA", "RotB",
        "AromaticRings", "RingCount", "HeavyAtoms", "FractionCSP3", "QED"]

rep = exact.loc[exact["n_measurements"] > 1]
sigma_exp = math.sqrt(np.nansum((rep["n_measurements"] - 1) * rep["pActivity_sd"] ** 2)
                      / np.nansum(rep["n_measurements"] - 1))
r2_ceiling = 1 - sigma_exp ** 2 / exact["pActivity"].var()

raw_sha = hashlib.sha256(data_path("rock1_chembl_curated.csv").read_bytes()).hexdigest()
print(f"curated table: {df.shape[0]} compounds x {df.shape[1]} columns; "
      f"{len(exact)} with at least one exact measurement, {int(df['censored'].sum())} censored")
print(f"replicates: {len(rep)} compounds measured more than once; "
      f"pooled experimental sd sigma_exp = {sigma_exp:.3f} log units -> R2 ceiling about {r2_ceiling:.2f}")
print("SHA-256 of the curated file:", raw_sha[:32], "...")

curated table: 4280 compounds x 33 columns; 2764 with at least one exact measurement, 1516 censored
replicates: 375 compounds measured more than once; pooled experimental sd sigma_exp = 0.506 log units -> R2 ceiling about 0.79
SHA-256 of the curated file: 765ab0cf633b4dd26a9be200f21c7972 ...

The pooled standard deviation printed above is the number against which every performance metric in this unit must be read. It is the spread between repeated measurements of the same compound in the public literature, so no model — however good — can predict this data set with a root-mean-square error much below it[34]. Unit 6 derived it in detail; it is recomputed here because a paper may not quote a number it did not produce.

Now the model. It is the running model of the course, built on the ChEMBL snapshot described in Unit 3[26]: Morgan fingerprints (radius 2, 2,048 bits) concatenated with eleven RDKit descriptors, a random forest[27] of 200 trees, evaluated twice — under a random five-fold cross-validation and under a Bemis–Murcko scaffold hold-out[35] in which no scaffold appears on both sides of the split. Reporting both is the whole point: the first number is what an optimistic paper quotes, the second is what the model will do on new chemistry.

# Fit the model twice: random 5-fold CV and a scaffold hold-out. ~40 s.
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold, cross_val_predict

gen = rdFingerprintGenerator.GetMorganGenerator(radius=2, fpSize=2048)
mols = [Chem.MolFromSmiles(s) for s in exact["std_smiles"]]
Xfp = np.array([gen.GetFingerprintAsNumPy(m) for m in mols], dtype=np.float32)
X = np.hstack([Xfp, exact[DESC].to_numpy(float)])
y = exact["pActivity"].to_numpy()
scaf = exact["scaffold_smiles"].to_numpy()

HP = dict(n_estimators=200, random_state=SEED, n_jobs=4)   # every hyperparameter of the reported model

def scaffold_holdout(scaffolds, frac_train=0.8):
    '''Largest Bemis-Murcko families to training, rarest to test; deterministic, no scaffold shared.'''
    groups = pd.Series(scaffolds).groupby(scaffolds).groups
    order = sorted(groups.values(), key=lambda g: (-len(g), str(scaffolds[g[0]])))
    tr, te = [], []
    n_tr = int(frac_train * len(scaffolds))
    for g in order:
        (tr if len(tr) < n_tr else te).extend(list(g))
    return np.array(tr), np.array(te)

rf = RandomForestRegressor(**HP)
pred_cv = cross_val_predict(rf, X, y, cv=KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED), n_jobs=1)
rmse_cv = float(np.sqrt(np.mean((pred_cv - y) ** 2)))
r2_cv = float(1 - np.sum((pred_cv - y) ** 2) / np.sum((y - y.mean()) ** 2))

TR, TE = scaffold_holdout(scaf)
rf.fit(X[TR], y[TR])
pred_te = rf.predict(X[TE])
rmse_sc = float(np.sqrt(np.mean((pred_te - y[TE]) ** 2)))
mae_sc = float(np.mean(np.abs(pred_te - y[TE])))
r2_sc = float(1 - np.sum((pred_te - y[TE]) ** 2) / np.sum((y[TE] - y[TE].mean()) ** 2))

print(f"random 5-fold CV   : RMSE {rmse_cv:.3f}   R2 {r2_cv:.3f}   (n = {len(y)})")
print(f"scaffold hold-out  : RMSE {rmse_sc:.3f}   MAE {mae_sc:.3f}   R2 {r2_sc:.3f} "
      f"(train {len(TR)} / test {len(TE)}, shared scaffolds {len(set(scaf[TR]) & set(scaf[TE]))})")
print(f"experimental floor : sigma_exp {sigma_exp:.3f}")

random 5-fold CV   : RMSE 0.727   R2 0.570   (n = 2764)
scaffold hold-out  : RMSE 0.851   MAE 0.659   R2 0.324 (train 2211 / test 553, shared scaffolds 0)
experimental floor : sigma_exp 0.506

Two numbers, one model, a difference of roughly a tenth of a log unit in RMSE and of a quarter in $R^2$. Which one goes in the abstract is the most consequential writing decision in a QSAR paper, and the answer is: both, with the claim attached to the pessimistic one. A paper quoting only the random-split figure answers a question nobody asked — how well the model interpolates among chemotypes it has already seen.

2. The figure as a physical object

A figure in a manuscript is printed at a fixed physical width: one column (about 8.5 cm in most chemistry and biology journals), one and a half columns (about 11.4 cm) or the full page width (about 17.4 cm). Everything else follows from that number. If you draw a figure at matplotlib's default 6.4 × 4.8 inches and the journal shrinks it to 8.5 cm, every font in it shrinks by a factor of 0.52, and a 10-point axis label arrives at the reader as 5 points — below the minimum of 5–7 points that most publishers specify. The fix is not to enlarge the fonts afterwards; it is to draw the figure at its final size from the start and never scale it again[1].

The second physical property is resolution. Raster formats (PNG, TIFF) store pixels and must be generated at the publisher's dpi — typically 300 dpi for photographs and 600–1200 dpi for line art. Vector formats (PDF, SVG, EPS) store drawing instructions and are resolution-independent: a scatter plot, a line chart or a bar chart should always be vector. The exception is a figure with tens of thousands of marks — a scatter of 100,000 docking poses will produce a 40 MB PDF that crashes the typesetter — where rasterising only the heavy artist (rasterized=True) inside an otherwise vector figure is the professional compromise.

The third is fonts. A PDF that references a font without embedding it renders differently on the publisher's machine, and matplotlib's default PDF font type (Type 3) is rejected by several publishers; setting pdf.fonttype = 42 and ps.fonttype = 42 once in the stylesheet fixes it permanently. The cell below writes the same figure in four ways and measures the consequences.

# A figure's physical properties, measured: format, dpi, file size, font embedding.
CM = 1 / 2.54                      # matplotlib thinks in inches; journals think in centimetres
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)

def demo_axes(ax):
    ax.scatter(exact["MolWt"], exact["pActivity"], s=4, alpha=0.25, color="#2b6cb0", rasterized=False)
    ax.set_xlabel("Molecular weight (Da)"); ax.set_ylabel("pActivity (-log$_{10}$ M)")
    ax.set_title("ROCK1 compounds")

matplotlib.rcParams["pdf.fonttype"] = 42      # TrueType, embeddable and editable
matplotlib.rcParams["ps.fonttype"] = 42

sizes = {}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5 * CM, 6.0 * CM))
demo_axes(ax)
for name, kw in [("fig_col.png", dict(dpi=150)), ("fig_col_300.png", dict(dpi=300)),
                 ("fig_col.pdf", {}), ("fig_col.svg", {})]:
    fig.savefig(WORK / name, bbox_inches="tight", **kw)
    sizes[name] = (WORK / name).stat().st_size / 1024
plt.close(fig)

pdf_bytes = (WORK / "fig_col.pdf").read_bytes()
embedded = b"/FontFile" in pdf_bytes or b"/FontFile2" in pdf_bytes or b"/FontFile3" in pdf_bytes
for name, kb in sizes.items():
    print(f"{name:<16} {kb:8.1f} kB")
print(f"\nfonts embedded in the PDF: {embedded}  (searched for /FontFile in {len(pdf_bytes)/1024:.0f} kB)")
print(f"one-column width 8.5 cm = {8.5*CM:.2f} in; full width 17.4 cm = {17.4*CM:.2f} in")

fig_col.png          68.6 kB
fig_col_300.png     207.5 kB
fig_col.pdf          70.8 kB
fig_col.svg         427.6 kB

fonts embedded in the PDF: True  (searched for /FontFile in 71 kB)
one-column width 8.5 cm = 3.35 in; full width 17.4 cm = 6.85 in

The PDF is the smallest of the four files and the only one that stays sharp at any magnification, because it stores roughly two thousand circle instructions rather than a grid of pixels; the 300 dpi PNG is several times larger and still blurs when the reader zooms. The /FontFile check is worth keeping in a submission script: it is the difference between a figure that renders identically everywhere and one that silently substitutes a font on the publisher's system.

Exercise 1

Re-run the cell above with rasterized=True in demo_axes and compare the PDF size. Then increase the number of points tenfold by plotting the full df (including censored compounds) and compare again. At what point does rasterising the data layer become the right decision, and what do you lose when you make it?

3. The same axes at two sizes: why figsize is not a detail

The clearest way to internalise the sizing rule is to see it fail. The next figure draws identical content twice, once at one-column width and once at full-page width, with the same font settings, and places them side by side at the same display scale — exactly what the typesetter does to your figure.

# The same plot drawn at 8.5 cm and at 17.4 cm, shown at the same display scale.
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(9.0, 3.4))
for i, (w_cm, label) in enumerate([(8.5, "one column (8.5 cm)"), (17.4, "full page (17.4 cm)")]):
    sub = fig.add_subplot(1, 2, i + 1)
    sub.axis("off")
    # an inset whose size is proportional to the physical width it stands for
    scale = w_cm / 17.4
    box = sub.inset_axes([0.5 - 0.5 * scale, 0.5 - 0.5 * scale * 0.72, scale, scale * 0.72])
    box.scatter(exact["MolWt"], exact["pActivity"], s=3, alpha=0.2, color="#2b6cb0")
    box.set_xlabel("Molecular weight (Da)", fontsize=9)
    box.set_ylabel("pActivity", fontsize=9)
    box.tick_params(labelsize=8)
    sub.set_title(f"{label}\n9 pt labels become {9*scale:.1f} pt relative to the page", fontsize=9)
fig.suptitle("Identical font settings, two final widths", fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
print(f"a 9 pt label in a figure drawn at 17.4 cm and printed at 8.5 cm arrives as {9*8.5/17.4:.1f} pt")

a 9 pt label in a figure drawn at 17.4 cm and printed at 8.5 cm arrives as 4.4 pt

Figure 1. The same scatter of molecular weight against pActivity rendered for two final widths. The right-hand panel was drawn at full-page width and is reproduced here at the same page scale as the left-hand one; its 9-point labels arrive at about 4.4 points, below every publisher's minimum. The content is identical: only the declared figsize differs. Draw at the final width, choose the font size once, and never scale the figure again.

4. A stylesheet, not a hundred keyword arguments

Consistency across the figures of one paper is itself a quality signal, and it is impossible to achieve by passing keyword arguments at each call site. matplotlib reads its defaults from rcParams, a dictionary that can be set globally, written to a .mplstyle file and shipped with the manuscript's repository. The laboratory's style below is deliberately austere: no top or right spines, a small sans-serif font, light grid only on the value axis, a colour-blind-safe categorical cycle, TrueType fonts in PDF, and a figure size expressed in centimetres.

# The laboratory stylesheet, written to a file and applied as a context manager.
OKABE_ITO = ["#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#009E73", "#CC79A7", "#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#F0E442", "#000000"]
LAB_STYLE = {
    "figure.figsize": (8.5 * CM, 6.0 * CM), "figure.dpi": 150, "savefig.dpi": 600,
    "savefig.bbox": "tight", "savefig.pad_inches": 0.02,
    "pdf.fonttype": 42, "ps.fonttype": 42, "svg.fonttype": "none",
    "font.family": "sans-serif", "font.size": 8, "axes.titlesize": 8, "axes.labelsize": 8,
    "axes.titleweight": "bold", "xtick.labelsize": 7, "ytick.labelsize": 7, "legend.fontsize": 7,
    "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False, "axes.linewidth": 0.8,
    "xtick.direction": "out", "ytick.direction": "out", "lines.linewidth": 1.2,
    "lines.markersize": 3, "legend.frameon": False, "axes.grid": True, "grid.alpha": 0.25,
    "grid.linewidth": 0.5, "axes.axisbelow": True,
    "axes.prop_cycle": matplotlib.cycler(color=OKABE_ITO),
}
def style_line(key, value):
    '''Serialise one rcParam for a .mplstyle file: no parentheses, no leading # in colours.'''
    if key == "figure.figsize":
        return f"{key}: {value[0]:.3f}, {value[1]:.3f}"
    if key == "axes.prop_cycle":
        bare = [c.lstrip("#") for c in OKABE_ITO]      # '#' starts a comment in a style file
        return key + ": cycler('color', " + str(bare) + ")"
    return f"{key}: {value}"

style_file = WORK / "lbqc.mplstyle"
style_file.write_text("\n".join(style_line(k, v) for k, v in LAB_STYLE.items()) + "\n")
print(style_file.read_text()[:430], "...\n")
with plt.style.context(style_file):
    loaded_size = tuple(round(v, 3) for v in plt.rcParams["figure.figsize"])
    loaded_cycle = plt.rcParams["axes.prop_cycle"].by_key()["color"][:3]
print(f"{len(LAB_STYLE)} parameters fixed once; matplotlib exposes {len(matplotlib.rcParams)} in total")
print(f"file reloads cleanly: figsize {loaded_size} in, first colours {loaded_cycle}")
print("use it with:  with plt.style.context(style_file):  ...   or  plt.style.use(style_file)")

figure.figsize: 3.346, 2.362
figure.dpi: 150
savefig.dpi: 600
savefig.bbox: tight
savefig.pad_inches: 0.02
pdf.fonttype: 42
ps.fonttype: 42
svg.fonttype: none
font.family: sans-serif
font.size: 8
axes.titlesize: 8
axes.labelsize: 8
axes.titleweight: bold
xtick.labelsize: 7
ytick.labelsize: 7
legend.fontsize: 7

axes.spines.right: False
axes.linewidth: 0.8
xtick.direction: out
ytick.direction: out
lines.li ...

file reloads cleanly: figsize (3.346, 2.362) in, first colours ['#0072B2', '#D55E00', '#009E73']
use it with:  with plt.style.context(style_file):  ...   or  plt.style.use(style_file)

Two details are worth defending. svg.fonttype: none keeps text as text in the SVG, so a co-author can fix a typo without redrawing the glyphs — the only manual edit the laboratory tolerates. And savefig.dpi: 600 applies to raster output only; the on-screen figure.dpi stays low so the notebook remains responsive. The serialiser above exists because a .mplstyle file is not Python: a figure size is written as two bare numbers, and a # begins a comment, so hexadecimal colours must lose their leading hash or the rest of the line is silently discarded — a failure that produces no error and a figure in the wrong colours.

5. Remaking an exploratory figure as a publication figure

Here is the worked case. Unit 5 produced an exploratory figure while looking for structure in the ROCK1 table: molecular weight against pActivity, coloured by a third variable, with default styling and no thought given to overplotting. It did its job — it was looked at once, by one person, for ten seconds. Printed in a paper it would be unreadable and, worse, misleading: with 2,764 semi-transparent points, the eye sees the outline of the cloud rather than its density, and a rainbow colour map makes a continuous variable look like it has bands.

The remake applies six changes, each of which can be justified to a referee: final size and font set by the stylesheet; overplotting solved by binning rather than transparency; the colour map replaced by a perceptually uniform one[6][7]; a second panel that shows the quantity the paper actually claims (predicted against observed under the scaffold split) instead of a descriptive correlation; reference lines that encode the claim (the identity line and the experimental error band); and panel letters so the caption can refer to them.

# BEFORE: the exploratory figure, exactly as an EDA cell produces it.
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 4.8))                     # matplotlib default size
sc = ax.scatter(exact["MolWt"], exact["pActivity"], c=exact["MolLogP"],
                cmap="jet", alpha=0.6, s=25)                   # rainbow map, heavy overplotting
ax.set_xlabel("MolWt"); ax.set_ylabel("pActivity")             # no units, abbreviated names
ax.set_title("MolWt vs pActivity colored by MolLogP")
fig.colorbar(sc)
plt.show()
print(f"{len(exact)} points drawn on {6.4*4.8:.0f} square inches; "
      f"Pearson r(MolWt, pActivity) = {np.corrcoef(exact['MolWt'], exact['pActivity'])[0,1]:+.3f}")

2764 points drawn on 31 square inches; Pearson r(MolWt, pActivity) = +0.077

Figure 2. The exploratory version. Three defects matter for print: the figure is drawn at 6.4 × 4.8 inches and would be reduced by half, the jet colour map invents visual boundaries in a smooth variable and is unreadable in greyscale, and the 2,764 overlapping markers hide the density where the data are densest. The correlation printed beneath it is weak, which is itself the finding this panel should communicate — and does not.

Now the publication version of the same evidence.

# AFTER: a two-panel publication figure built with the laboratory stylesheet.
with plt.style.context(style_file):
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(17.4 * CM, 7.0 * CM), layout="constrained")

    ax = axes[0]
    hb = ax.hexbin(exact["MolWt"], exact["pActivity"], gridsize=38, cmap="viridis",
                   mincnt=1, linewidths=0.0)
    med = exact.groupby(pd.cut(exact["MolWt"], np.arange(150, 751, 50)),
                        observed=True)["pActivity"].median()
    centres = [iv.mid for iv in med.index]
    ax.plot(centres, med.values, color="#D55E00", lw=1.4, marker="o", ms=3, label="median per 50 Da bin")
    ax.set_xlabel("Molecular weight (Da)")
    ax.set_ylabel("pActivity ($-\\log_{10}$ M)")
    ax.set_xlim(150, 750)
    ax.legend(loc="lower right")
    cb = fig.colorbar(hb, ax=ax, pad=0.02); cb.set_label("compounds per bin", fontsize=7)
    cb.ax.tick_params(labelsize=6)

    ax = axes[1]
    ax.scatter(y[TE], pred_te, s=5, alpha=0.5, color="#0072B2", edgecolors="none")
    lo, hi = 3.3, 10.2
    ax.plot([lo, hi], [lo, hi], color="black", lw=0.9)
    ax.fill_between([lo, hi], [lo - sigma_exp, hi - sigma_exp], [lo + sigma_exp, hi + sigma_exp],
                    color="grey", alpha=0.18, lw=0, label=f"$\\pm\\sigma_{{exp}}$ = {sigma_exp:.2f}")
    ax.set_xlim(lo, hi); ax.set_ylim(lo, hi); ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.set_xlabel("Observed pActivity"); ax.set_ylabel("Predicted pActivity")
    ax.legend(loc="upper left")
    ax.text(0.97, 0.06, f"RMSE {rmse_sc:.2f}\n$R^2$ {r2_sc:.2f}\nn = {len(TE)}",
            transform=ax.transAxes, ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=7)

    for ax, letter in zip(axes, "AB"):
        ax.text(-0.14, 1.04, letter, transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")

plt.show()
print("saved", (WORK / 'figure1.pdf').name, f"{(WORK/'figure1.pdf').stat().st_size/1024:.0f} kB,",
      f"drawn at 17.4 x 7.0 cm; densest hexagon holds {int(hb.get_array().max())} compounds")

Figure 3. The publication remake. (A) Density of the 2,764 exact-value ROCK1 compounds in the molecular-weight / potency plane, binned into hexagons so that the colour encodes how many compounds occupy each region; the orange line is the median potency per 50 Da bin and is nearly flat across the range, which is the honest reading of a correlation below +0.1. (B) Predicted against observed pActivity for the scaffold hold-out set, with the identity line and a grey band of one experimental standard deviation; the model's scaffold-split RMSE is printed in the panel. Both panels were produced by the code shown, at 17.4 × 7.0 cm, with fonts and colours fixed by the laboratory stylesheet.

Compare the two captions. The exploratory caption describes what is plotted; the publication caption describes what is plotted, states the sample size, names the statistical object (median per bin, identity line, error band) and tells the reader what to conclude. That is the caption contract: a caption must let a reader who skipped the text understand the panel, and it must not assert anything the panel does not show.

6. Colour, accessibility and the greyscale test

Roughly one man in twelve and one woman in two hundred has a colour-vision deficiency, most often a reduced ability to distinguish red from green. A figure that encodes its only distinction in red versus green is unreadable to them, and a figure printed in greyscale — which still happens, and always happens when a reader photocopies a page — is unreadable to everyone if its categories differ only in hue. Two rules remove the whole problem: use a perceptually uniform sequential map (viridis, cividis, magma) for continuous variables, and a categorical palette designed for colour-vision deficiency, such as the Okabe–Ito set used in the stylesheet above[8], for discrete ones — plus a second channel (marker shape, line style) whenever the distinction carries the claim[6].

The cell below simulates deuteranopia with a standard linear transformation of the sRGB values and converts the same colours to luminance, so that the failure can be seen rather than taken on faith.

# Simulate deuteranopia and greyscale for two categorical palettes and two colour maps.
from matplotlib.colors import to_rgb
DEUTER = np.array([[0.625, 0.375, 0.0], [0.70, 0.30, 0.0], [0.0, 0.30, 0.70]])   # Vienot-style approximation
def simulate(colours, kind):
    rgb = np.array([to_rgb(c) for c in colours])
    if kind == "deuteranopia":
        return np.clip(rgb @ DEUTER.T, 0, 1)
    lum = rgb @ np.array([0.2126, 0.7152, 0.0722])
    return np.repeat(lum[:, None], 3, axis=1)

BAD = ["#B22222", "#556B2F", "#CD5C5C", "#6B8E23", "#A0522D", "#2E6B2E"]   # red/green, matched lightness
palettes = {"red/green palette (bad)": BAD, "Okabe-Ito palette (good)": OKABE_ITO[:6],
            "jet colour map (bad)": [plt.get_cmap("jet")(v) for v in np.linspace(0, 1, 6)],
            "viridis colour map (good)": [plt.get_cmap("viridis")(v) for v in np.linspace(0, 1, 6)]}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 3, figsize=(9.0, 4.6), layout="constrained")
for r, (name, cols) in enumerate(palettes.items()):
    for c, kind in enumerate(["original", "deuteranopia", "greyscale"]):
        ax = axes[r, c]
        shown = np.array([to_rgb(x) for x in cols]) if kind == "original" else simulate(cols, kind)
        ax.imshow(shown[None, :, :], aspect="auto")
        ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
        if c == 0: ax.set_ylabel(name, fontsize=7, rotation=0, ha="right", va="center")
        if r == 0: ax.set_title(kind, fontsize=9)
plt.show()
d = simulate(BAD[:2], "deuteranopia")
d2 = simulate(OKABE_ITO[:2], "deuteranopia")
print(f"firebrick vs olive under deuteranopia: RGB {np.round(d[0],2)} vs {np.round(d[1],2)}, "
      f"distance {np.linalg.norm(d[0]-d[1]):.2f}")
print(f"Okabe-Ito blue vs vermillion under deuteranopia: distance {np.linalg.norm(d2[0]-d2[1]):.2f} "
      f"({np.linalg.norm(d2[0]-d2[1])/np.linalg.norm(d[0]-d[1]):.1f} times larger)")
gj = simulate([plt.get_cmap("jet")(v) for v in [0.16, 0.94]], "greyscale")
gv = simulate([plt.get_cmap("viridis")(v) for v in [0.16, 0.94]], "greyscale")
print(f"jet at 16% and 94% of its range: greyscale luminance {gj[0,0]:.3f} vs {gj[1,0]:.3f} "
      f"- two very different values printing as the same grey")
print(f"viridis at the same two positions: {gv[0,0]:.3f} vs {gv[1,0]:.3f}")

firebrick vs olive under deuteranopia: RGB [0.49 0.53 0.13] vs [0.37 0.36 0.25], distance 0.24
Okabe-Ito blue vs vermillion under deuteranopia: distance 0.91 (3.8 times larger)
jet at 16% and 94% of its range: greyscale luminance 0.163 vs 0.163 - two very different values printing as the same grey
viridis at the same two positions: 0.247 vs 0.822

Figure 4. Four palettes under three conditions. Rows one and three use colours that collapse: firebrick and olive, chosen with similar lightness, become nearly the same colour for a deuteranope, and the jet colour map is non-monotonic in luminance, so two values at opposite ends of its range print as the same grey. Rows two and four stay separable in all three columns. The printed numbers quantify it — the Okabe–Ito pair keeps several times the separation of the red/green pair under the same simulation, and viridis separates in greyscale where jet does not.

7. Figures that mislead, and the honest version of the same data

The most damaging figure is not the ugly one; it is the one that is beautiful and overstates the evidence. Three patterns account for most of it in computational papers: a truncated value axis that turns a small difference into a large one, a bar of means that hides the distribution it averages[5], and a dual-axis plot that invites the reader to see a correlation between two arbitrary scalings. The next cell builds the first two from real data — two scaffold families from the ROCK1 table — and puts the honest version beside each.

# A real, small difference presented three ways: two misleading, one honest.
counts = exact["scaffold_smiles"].value_counts()
fam = counts[counts >= 30].index                 # families large enough to compare
g1, g2 = fam[2], fam[3]                          # two of comparable size
a = exact.loc[exact["scaffold_smiles"] == g1, "pActivity"].to_numpy()
b = exact.loc[exact["scaffold_smiles"] == g2, "pActivity"].to_numpy()
diff = a.mean() - b.mean()
pooled_sd = math.sqrt(((len(a)-1)*a.var(ddof=1) + (len(b)-1)*b.var(ddof=1)) / (len(a)+len(b)-2))
cohen_d = diff / pooled_sd
boot = np.array([np.random.default_rng(i).choice(a, len(a)).mean()
                 - np.random.default_rng(1000+i).choice(b, len(b)).mean() for i in range(2000)])
ci = np.percentile(boot, [2.5, 97.5])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(9.5, 3.2), layout="constrained")
axes[0].bar(["scaffold A", "scaffold B"], [a.mean(), b.mean()], color=["#0072B2", "#D55E00"], width=0.5)
axes[0].set_ylim(min(a.mean(), b.mean()) - 0.05, max(a.mean(), b.mean()) + 0.05)
axes[0].set_ylabel("mean pActivity"); axes[0].set_title("truncated axis (misleading)")
axes[1].bar(["scaffold A", "scaffold B"], [a.mean(), b.mean()], color=["#0072B2", "#D55E00"], width=0.5,
            yerr=[a.std(ddof=1)/math.sqrt(len(a)), b.std(ddof=1)/math.sqrt(len(b))], capsize=3)
axes[1].set_ylim(0, 10); axes[1].set_ylabel("mean pActivity"); axes[1].set_title("bar of means (hides spread)")
parts = axes[2].violinplot([a, b], showextrema=False, widths=0.8)
for pc, col in zip(parts["bodies"], ["#0072B2", "#D55E00"]):
    pc.set_facecolor(col); pc.set_alpha(0.35)
for i, arr in enumerate([a, b], start=1):
    axes[2].scatter(np.full(len(arr), i) + np.random.default_rng(i).normal(0, 0.05, len(arr)),
                    arr, s=6, color="black", alpha=0.45)
axes[2].set_xticks([1, 2], [f"scaffold A\n(n={len(a)})", f"scaffold B\n(n={len(b)})"])
axes[2].set_ylabel("pActivity"); axes[2].set_title("distribution (honest)")
plt.show()
print(f"difference of means {diff:+.3f} log units, 95% bootstrap CI [{ci[0]:+.2f}, {ci[1]:+.2f}], "
      f"Cohen's d = {cohen_d:+.2f}")
print(f"apparent bar-height ratio with the truncated axis: "
      f"{(a.mean()-(min(a.mean(),b.mean())-0.05))/(b.mean()-(min(a.mean(),b.mean())-0.05)):.1f}x; "
      f"true ratio of the means: {a.mean()/b.mean():.2f}x")
print(f"experimental noise for a single compound is sigma_exp = {sigma_exp:.2f} log units, "
      f"{abs(sigma_exp/diff):.1f} times the difference being plotted")

difference of means +0.146 log units, 95% bootstrap CI [-0.18, +0.46], Cohen's d = +0.19
apparent bar-height ratio with the truncated axis: 3.9x; true ratio of the means: 1.02x
experimental noise for a single compound is sigma_exp = 0.51 log units, 3.5 times the difference being plotted

Figure 5. The same comparison between two Bemis–Murcko scaffold families of comparable size (43 and 38 compounds), drawn three ways. The left panel truncates the value axis and makes the left bar look several times the right one; the middle panel uses a full axis but replaces each distribution with a mean and a standard error, which hides that the two groups overlap almost completely; the right panel shows every compound. The printed statistics settle it: the difference of means is about 0.15 log units, its 95 % bootstrap confidence interval includes zero, Cohen's d is below 0.2, and the experimental noise of a single measurement is about three and a half times the difference being plotted.

This is the unit's failure-mode experiment, and it is worth being explicit about what failed. Nothing in the left panel is false: the bars are at the right heights, the axis is labelled, the data are real. The panel is dishonest because of what it omits — the zero, the spread and the sample size — and because the reader's visual system reads bar length as magnitude. The rule the laboratory applies is mechanical: bars start at zero or are not bars; a mean is never shown without its distribution or at least its confidence interval; and a difference is never plotted without the noise floor it must beat.

Exercise 2

Build the third misleading pattern yourself: plot the mean molecular weight and the mean pActivity of the compounds in each publication year — or, since this table has no year, in each decile of n_measurements — on a dual twinx() axis, and choose the two scalings so the curves appear to track each other. Then show the same data as two small multiples sharing an x-axis, and write the one-sentence caption that each version implies. Which of the two would you defend to a referee?

8. Multi-panel figures and the order in which they are read

A paper in our fields usually has four to six figures, and each one answers one question. Within a figure, panels are read left to right and top to bottom, and the reader assumes that this order is an argument: panel A establishes the setting, B shows the main evidence, C the control, D the consequence. Laying out panels that do not form such a sequence wastes the strongest convention you have.

Mechanically, multi-panel layouts in matplotlib[3] — whose object model descends from the grammar of graphics[4], so a panel is a composition of data, scales and marks rather than a picture — are solved by layout="constrained", which allocates space for labels and colour bars, and by subplot_mosaic, which describes panels of unequal size with a small text diagram. Panel letters go outside the axes, in bold, at a fixed offset set by code. The figure below is the Figure 1 of a hypothetical ROCK1 paper, assembled from objects this notebook has already computed.

# A four-panel Figure 1: data, model, error structure, decision.
resid = pred_te - y[TE]
with plt.style.context(style_file):
    fig, axd = plt.subplot_mosaic([["A", "B"], ["C", "D"]], figsize=(17.4 * CM, 12.0 * CM),
                                  layout="constrained")
    ax = axd["A"]
    ax.hist(exact["pActivity"], bins=40, color="#0072B2", alpha=0.85)
    ax.axvline(exact["pActivity"].median(), color="#D55E00", lw=1.2)
    ax.set_xlabel("pActivity ($-\\log_{10}$ M)"); ax.set_ylabel("compounds")
    ax.set_title("Potency distribution")

    ax = axd["B"]
    ax.scatter(y[TE], pred_te, s=4, alpha=0.45, color="#0072B2", edgecolors="none")
    ax.plot([3.3, 10.2], [3.3, 10.2], color="black", lw=0.8)
    ax.set_xlabel("Observed"); ax.set_ylabel("Predicted"); ax.set_title("Scaffold hold-out")
    ax.set_aspect("equal")

    ax = axd["C"]
    ax.hist(resid, bins=35, color="#009E73", alpha=0.85)
    ax.axvline(0, color="black", lw=0.8)
    for s in (-sigma_exp, sigma_exp):
        ax.axvline(s, color="#D55E00", lw=1.0, ls="--")
    ax.set_xlabel("Residual (log units)"); ax.set_ylabel("compounds")
    ax.set_title("Residuals vs experimental noise")

    ax = axd["D"]
    ks = np.arange(10, 210, 10)
    order = np.argsort(-pred_te)
    hits = np.array([(y[TE][order[:kk]] >= 7.0).sum() / kk for kk in ks])
    base = (y[TE] >= 7.0).mean()
    ax.plot(ks, hits, color="#0072B2", marker="o", ms=2.5, label="model ranking")
    ax.axhline(base, color="grey", ls=":", label=f"random baseline ({base:.2f})")
    ax.set_xlabel("Top-k compounds selected"); ax.set_ylabel("Fraction with pActivity $\\geq$ 7")
    ax.set_ylim(0, 1); ax.set_title("Enrichment of a selection"); ax.legend(loc="lower right")

    for letter, ax in axd.items():
        ax.text(-0.17, 1.06, letter, transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")
    fig.savefig(WORK / "figure2_fourpanel.pdf")
plt.show()
print(f"panel D: top-10 precision {hits[0]:.2f} vs baseline {base:.2f} "
      f"(enrichment {hits[0]/base:.1f}x); top-200 precision {hits[-1]:.2f}")
print(f"panel C: {100*np.mean(np.abs(resid) <= sigma_exp):.0f}% of residuals fall within one sigma_exp")

panel D: top-10 precision 0.80 vs baseline 0.19 (enrichment 4.2x); top-200 precision 0.41
panel C: 49% of residuals fall within one sigma_exp

Figure 6. A complete four-panel figure assembled from the analysis. (A) Distribution of measured potency over the 2,764 exact-value compounds, median marked. (B) Predicted against observed potency on the scaffold hold-out, identity line shown. (C) Residual distribution with dashed lines at plus and minus one experimental standard deviation; the fraction of residuals inside that band is printed below the figure. (D) Precision of the top-k ranked compounds against the base rate, the quantity that decides whether the model is useful for selecting compounds. The panels form an argument: this is the data, this is how well the model does on new scaffolds, this is how its error compares with the measurement itself, and this is what that buys when choosing compounds to test.

The convention extends to the figures themselves: Figure 1, the data; Figure 2, the method or its validation; Figure 3, the main result; Figure 4, the control that excludes the obvious alternative; Figure 5, the application. A figure that cannot be placed in that sequence usually belongs in the supplement. The diagram below sketches the same logic at the level of sentences.

the two red annotations are the two failures a referee is specifically looking for

Figure 7. The argument skeleton of a computational paper. The link from question to evidence is broken by a validation design that does not match the question — a random split used to support a claim about new chemotypes, or a feature computed before the split. The link from evidence to claim is broken by language: "accurately predicts" where the evidence supports "ranks better than chance within the applicability domain".

9. Tables, significant figures and the uncertainty that sets them

Tables are read more carefully than figures and written more carelessly. Three rules cover almost everything. Units go in the header, never in the cells. Columns are aligned on the decimal point, with the same number of decimals throughout a column. And significant figures are set by the uncertainty, not by the width of the float: printing RMSE = 0.8514371 claims one part in ten million for a quantity whose confidence interval is tenths wide.

The convention used in the physical sciences is: round the uncertainty to one significant figure (two if its leading digit is 1), then round the value to the same decimal place. Work the example by hand before writing the function.

quantity raw value raw uncertainty step 1: round the uncertainty step 2: match the value reported
scaffold RMSE 0.85143… 0.05468… 0.05 (1 s.f., leading digit 5) 2 decimals 0.85 ± 0.05
random-CV $R^2$ 0.57043… 0.01688… 0.017 (2 s.f., leading digit 1) 3 decimals 0.570 ± 0.017
top-10 precision 0.8 0.1265… 0.13 (2 s.f., leading digit 1) 2 decimals 0.80 ± 0.13

Rows two and three are the ones students get wrong: when the uncertainty begins with a 1, one significant figure would discard almost half the information in it, so two are kept. The next cell implements the rule and checks it against the table above.

# Significant figures tied to the uncertainty, worked by hand above and now by code.
def round_to_uncertainty(value, unc):
    '''Round unc to 1 s.f. (2 if its leading digit is 1) and value to the same decimal place.'''
    if unc <= 0 or not np.isfinite(unc):
        return f"{value:.3g}", ""
    exp = math.floor(math.log10(abs(unc)))
    lead = int(abs(unc) / 10 ** exp)
    sig = 2 if lead == 1 else 1
    dec = max(0, -(exp - (sig - 1)))
    unc_r = round(unc, dec)
    return f"{value:.{dec}f}", f"{unc_r:.{dec}f}"

checks = [("scaffold RMSE", 0.85143, 0.05468, "0.85", "0.05"),
          ("random-CV R2", 0.57043, 0.01688, "0.570", "0.017"),
          ("top-10 precision", 0.8, 0.12649, "0.80", "0.13")]
for name, v, u, ev, eu in checks:
    gv, gu = round_to_uncertainty(v, u)
    print(f"{name:<18} {v:.5f} +/- {u:.5f}  ->  {gv} +/- {gu}   "
          f"{'matches the hand-worked table' if (gv, gu) == (ev, eu) else 'MISMATCH'}")

scaffold RMSE      0.85143 +/- 0.05468  ->  0.85 +/- 0.05   matches the hand-worked table
random-CV R2       0.57043 +/- 0.01688  ->  0.570 +/- 0.017   matches the hand-worked table
top-10 precision   0.80000 +/- 0.12649  ->  0.80 +/- 0.13   matches the hand-worked table

The rule needs an uncertainty, so a performance table needs confidence intervals. For a hold-out metric the cheap and honest answer is a bootstrap over the test compounds: resample with replacement, recompute the metric, take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. It measures the uncertainty due to which compounds happened to be in the test set — not the uncertainty due to the choice of split, which is larger and is addressed by repeating the split.

# Bootstrap confidence intervals for the reported metrics, and the performance table.
def boot_ci(fn, n_boot=2000, seed=SEED):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    n = len(y[TE])
    vals = [fn(rng.integers(0, n, n)) for _ in range(n_boot)]
    return float(np.mean(vals)), np.percentile(vals, [2.5, 97.5])

yt, pt = y[TE], pred_te
m_rmse, ci_rmse = boot_ci(lambda ix: np.sqrt(np.mean((pt[ix] - yt[ix]) ** 2)))
m_mae, ci_mae = boot_ci(lambda ix: np.mean(np.abs(pt[ix] - yt[ix])))
m_r2, ci_r2 = boot_ci(lambda ix: 1 - np.sum((pt[ix]-yt[ix])**2) / np.sum((yt[ix]-yt[ix].mean())**2))
m_sp, ci_sp = boot_ci(lambda ix: scipy.stats.spearmanr(pt[ix], yt[ix]).statistic)

rows = []
for label, val, ci in [("RMSE (log units)", rmse_sc, ci_rmse), ("MAE (log units)", mae_sc, ci_mae),
                       ("R2", r2_sc, ci_r2), ("Spearman rho", scipy.stats.spearmanr(pt, yt).statistic, ci_sp)]:
    half = (ci[1] - ci[0]) / 2
    v, u = round_to_uncertainty(val, half)
    rows.append(dict(Metric=label, Value=v, **{"95% CI": f"[{ci[0]:.2f}, {ci[1]:.2f}]"},
                     **{"+/-": u}))
perf = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(perf.to_string(index=False))
print(f"\nfor comparison, the experimental floor is sigma_exp = {sigma_exp:.2f} log units; "
      f"the model's MAE is {mae_sc/sigma_exp:.2f} times it")

          Metric Value       95% CI  +/-
RMSE (log units)  0.85 [0.80, 0.91] 0.05
 MAE (log units)  0.66 [0.61, 0.70] 0.05
              R2  0.32 [0.24, 0.39] 0.08
    Spearman rho  0.57 [0.51, 0.63] 0.06

for comparison, the experimental floor is sigma_exp = 0.51 log units; the model's MAE is 1.30 times it

Table 1. Performance of the random-forest model on the scaffold hold-out set (n = 553 compounds), with 95 % bootstrap confidence intervals over 2,000 resamples of the test set. Values are rounded to the decimal implied by their own uncertainty. The MAE is close to the pooled experimental standard deviation of the data, which is the correct reference point for judging whether the model is worth deploying.

A performance table is also the place where metric cherry-picking happens. Reporting $R^2$ alone, on the split that flatters the model, is the most common form; reporting only $R^2$ at all is nearly as bad, because $R^2$ depends on the variance of the test set and so changes when the split changes even if the errors do not. Report an error in the units of the target (RMSE and MAE in log units), one rank metric, the sample size and the split. The figure below shows why: the same model, three evaluation protocols, three different stories.

# One model, several evaluation protocols: a forest plot with the experimental floor.
protocols = {"random 5-fold CV": rmse_cv, "scaffold hold-out": rmse_sc}
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
cv_boot = [np.sqrt(np.mean((pred_cv[ix] - y[ix]) ** 2))
           for ix in (rng.integers(0, len(y), len(y)) for _ in range(1000))]
ci_cvr = np.percentile(cv_boot, [2.5, 97.5])
dummy = np.sqrt(np.mean((y - y.mean()) ** 2))

labels = ["mean-prediction baseline", "random 5-fold CV", "scaffold hold-out"]
vals = [dummy, rmse_cv, rmse_sc]
cis = [(dummy, dummy), tuple(ci_cvr), tuple(ci_rmse)]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.6, 2.9))
ypos = np.arange(len(labels))[::-1]
for yy, v, (lo, hi) in zip(ypos, vals, cis):
    ax.plot([lo, hi], [yy, yy], color="#0072B2", lw=2)
    ax.plot(v, yy, "o", color="#0072B2", ms=6)
    ax.text(v, yy + 0.18, f"{v:.3f}", ha="center", fontsize=8)
ax.axvline(sigma_exp, color="#D55E00", ls="--", lw=1.2)
ax.text(sigma_exp + 0.01, -0.45, f"experimental floor {sigma_exp:.2f}", color="#D55E00", fontsize=8)
ax.set_yticks(ypos, labels); ax.set_xlabel("RMSE (log units)"); ax.set_xlim(0, 1.25)
ax.set_title("The same model under three protocols")
plt.show()
print(f"baseline {dummy:.3f} | random CV {rmse_cv:.3f} [{ci_cvr[0]:.3f}, {ci_cvr[1]:.3f}] | "
      f"scaffold {rmse_sc:.3f} [{ci_rmse[0]:.3f}, {ci_rmse[1]:.3f}]")
print(f"choosing the random-CV number over the scaffold number improves the headline by "
      f"{100*(rmse_sc-rmse_cv)/rmse_sc:.0f}% without changing the model")

baseline 1.108 | random CV 0.727 [0.703, 0.750] | scaffold 0.851 [0.797, 0.906]
choosing the random-CV number over the scaffold number improves the headline by 15% without changing the model

Figure 8. Root-mean-square error of one random forest under three protocols, with 95 % bootstrap intervals and the experimental noise floor as a dashed line. The baseline is the error of predicting the training mean for everything. The gap between the random cross-validation and the scaffold hold-out is a property of the evaluation, not of the model; a paper that quotes only the left-hand point improves its headline number by about a sixth while telling the reader nothing about new chemotypes.

10. From a DataFrame to LaTeX, Word and a machine-readable supplement

Three destinations, three formats, one source of truth. The DataFrame is the source; everything else is generated. to_latex with booktabs produces a table that compiles unmodified in a journal template; to_markdown produces a table that can be pasted into a Word manuscript or a GitHub README; and the supplement is a CSV — not a spreadsheet — with a companion data dictionary, because a .xlsx file converts gene symbols into dates and compound identifiers into floats[30].

# One DataFrame, three exports.

                               "set (n = 553), with 95\\% bootstrap confidence intervals."),
                      label="tab:performance")
print(latex)
print(perf.to_markdown(index=False))

Three things make that supplement reusable rather than decorative: a stable identifier (the InChIKey) to join on, the structure itself so the join works for a reader who does not use InChIKeys, and a data dictionary naming the type, unit and provenance of every column. The checksum goes in the repository manifest, so a file downloaded two years later can be shown to be the file that was published.

11. A Methods section that permits replication

The test of a Methods section is simple and brutal: could a competent stranger, with your data and no access to you, obtain your numbers? For a computational paper that requires five classes of information — the data and its provenance, the preprocessing, the model and every hyperparameter that is not a default, the validation protocol, and the software environment with versions and seeds[14][17]. All five are available inside the notebook that did the work, so the paragraph can be generated instead of remembered.

# Generate the Methods paragraph from the provenance the notebook already holds.
METHODS_LINES = [

Data. Bioactivity data for human ROCK1 (ChEMBL target CHEMBL3231, UniProt Q13464) were retrieved from
ChEMBL release 37 (2026-05-01) restricted to IC50, Ki and Kd measurements, giving 5,089 activity records.
Records without a structure, with a ChEMBL data-validity flag, without a numeric standard value, or outside
the 3-70 heavy-atom window were removed. Structures were standardised with RDKit 2026.03.4
(Normalizer, LargestFragmentChooser, Uncharger) and keyed by InChIKey; measurements of the same parent
structure were aggregated by the median of the exact (relation '=') values, yielding 4280 compounds,
of which 2764 have at least one exact measurement and 1516 are censored and
were excluded from regression. Activities are reported as pActivity = -log10(activity in M). The pooled
within-compound standard deviation over the 375 replicated compounds is 0.51 log units,
which we take as the experimental error floor. The curated table (SHA-256
765ab0cf633b4dd2...) is deposited with the code.

Descriptors. Each compound was represented by a Morgan fingerprint (radius 2, 2,048 bits, RDKit
MorganGenerator) concatenated with 11 RDKit physicochemical descriptors (MolWt, MolLogP, TPSA, HBD, HBA, RotB, AromaticRings, RingCount, HeavyAtoms, FractionCSP3, QED),
giving 2059 features. No feature scaling was applied, as the model is tree-based.

Model and validation. A random-forest regressor (scikit-learn 1.9.0;
n_estimators=200, all other hyperparameters at library defaults, random_state=0) was
evaluated in two ways: (i) five-fold cross-validation with shuffling (random_state=0) over all
2764 compounds, and (ii) a Bemis-Murcko scaffold hold-out in which the largest scaffold families
(2211 compounds) form the training set and the remaining 553 compounds the test set, with no
scaffold shared between them. Metrics are RMSE, MAE, R2 and Spearman rho; 95% confidence intervals were
obtained by bootstrapping the test compounds 2,000 times (numpy default_rng, seed 0).

Software. Python 3.11.15, numpy 2.4.6, pandas 3.0.3,
scipy 1.17.1, scikit-learn 1.9.0, RDKit 2026.03.4,
matplotlib 3.11.0. All random seeds were fixed at 0. The analysis notebook that
produced every number and figure in this work is available in the repository cited below.

[316 words]

Read that paragraph as a referee. Every number in it is a variable from the analysis, so it cannot drift from the results. It names the release of the database, not just the database, and states which rows were excluded and why — censored compounds are the kind of silent exclusion that invalidates comparisons between papers. It gives the hyperparameters that were set and says the rest are library defaults, the only honest way to describe a model with forty parameters. And it states a seed, which converts "we obtained" into "anyone obtains".

What it does not do is justify the choices; that belongs in the Results or the Discussion. A Methods section is a recipe, not an argument. One omission is worth repairing by hand: the libraries that did the work should be cited as software, not merely named — NumPy[29], scikit-learn[28] and matplotlib[3] all have citable papers, and Unit 24 returns to software citation as an obligation rather than a courtesy.

Exercise 3

Delete one sentence from the generated Methods and ask a classmate to reproduce the scaffold hold-out RMSE from what remains. Repeat with a different sentence removed. Rank the sentences by how much damage their removal does; the top three are the ones referees ask about, and the exercise is a cheap simulation of peer review.

12. The reporting checklists the laboratory is held to

Four communities the group publishes in have written down what a paper must report. They overlap, they are short, and filling one in takes twenty minutes — which is the best-value twenty minutes in the whole writing process, because every item a checklist flags is an item a referee would have flagged later.

OECD principles and the QMRF. The five OECD principles for the validation of (Q)SAR models[12][13] are the legal and practical baseline for regulatory and academic QSAR: a defined endpoint, an unambiguous algorithm, a defined applicability domain, appropriate measures of goodness-of-fit, robustness and predictivity, and — where possible — a mechanistic interpretation. The QMRF (QSAR Model Reporting Format) is the structured document that records them.

# OECD principles, filled in for the model fitted in this notebook.
oecd = pd.DataFrame([

Two of the five are only partly met, and saying so is the point: a checklist with five green ticks for a notebook-grade model is decoration. The QMRF itself has nine sections — identifier, general information, endpoint, algorithm, applicability domain, internal and external validation, mechanistic interpretation, miscellaneous — and the laboratory keeps one per published model, generated like the Methods paragraph above.

TRIPOD+AI applies when the prediction target is a clinical outcome in people[10]. It is the checklist for the group's biomedical projects — the periodontitis expression data of Unit 21, say, if it were used to predict disease status — and it is not a QSAR checklist. Students routinely try to apply all four checklists to everything, which produces a long table of "not applicable" entries and hides the handful of items that matter. The cell below fills in the subset of TRIPOD+AI items that a computational chemistry paper would still be judged on, and marks the rest honestly.

MIAME and MINSEQE are the minimum-information standards for microarray and sequencing experiments[11]: raw data, processed data, sample annotation, experimental design, protocol and array/platform description, deposited in a public repository (GEO, ArrayExpress) with an accession that the paper quotes. LiveCoMS best practices play the same role for molecular simulation[15][16]: report the force field and its version, the water model, the thermostat and barostat with their coupling constants, the integration time step, the equilibration protocol, the number and length of independent replicas, and an uncertainty estimate that accounts for correlation in time.

13. Availability, licences and preprints

Two short statements at the end of a paper do more for its reuse than any amount of Discussion. A data-availability statement says where the data are, under what identifier, and what a reader must do to get them; "available from the authors on reasonable request" is, empirically, a statement that the data are not available[20][21]. The target is the FAIR standard — findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable[18] — and the incentive is not only ethical: papers with openly deposited data are cited measurably more often[19]. A code-availability statement names a repository, a release tag or commit and, ideally, an archival DOI from a service such as Zenodo, because a GitHub repository can be deleted and a DOI cannot.

Licences are where the laboratory's own obligations appear. ChEMBL data are distributed under CC BY-SA 3.0, a share-alike licence: a curated table derived from ChEMBL must be redistributed under the same terms, and quietly putting it under CC BY or under no licence at all is a licence violation, not an oversight. Code in the group is released under the MIT licence unless a dependency forces otherwise, and figures under CC BY 4.0.

# The statements, generated with the identifiers they must contain.
AVAIL_LINES = [
 "Data availability. The curated ROCK1 activity table analysed in this study was derived from ChEMBL release",
 "37 (target CHEMBL3231, accessed 2026-10-18) and is deposited with the analysis code (file",

A preprint is the third element. Posting to ChemRxiv, bioRxiv or arXiv at submission establishes priority and makes the work citable while it is in review; almost every journal the laboratory targets permits it, and the exceptions are listed in the journal's policy page, to be checked before posting rather than after.

14. The abstract, and the ladder of claims

The abstract is read a hundred times for every time the paper is read, so it is written last and rewritten most. A structured four-move abstract fits any computational paper: what problem and why it matters (two sentences), what was done (two sentences, with the data size), what was found (two or three sentences, with the key numbers and their uncertainty), and what it means and for whom (one sentence, bounded by the applicability domain). The hardest discipline is the last move, because it is where over-claiming lives.

The ladder of claims is a device the group uses in internal review. For any result, write the claim at four strengths and choose the highest one the evidence supports: (1) "we observed", (2) "the model ranks", (3) "the model predicts", (4) "the model enables". Evidence of a scaffold-split RMSE just above the experimental noise floor supports rung two comfortably, rung three with the domain stated, and rung four not at all without prospective validation.

# A generated abstract, and a count of the things an editor checks.
ABSTRACT_LINES = [
 "Rho-associated kinase 1 (ROCK1) is a therapeutic target in glaucoma, fibrosis and cardiovascular disease,",
 "and public bioactivity data for it are large enough to support ligand-based models but heterogeneous enough",
 f"to mislead them. We curated {len(df)} compounds with measured ROCK1 affinity from ChEMBL 37 ({len(exact)}",
 "with exact values) and estimated the experimental error floor of the data at",
 f"{sigma_exp:.2f} log units from replicate measurements. A random forest on Morgan fingerprints and",
 f"physicochemical descriptors reached an RMSE of {rmse_cv:.2f} log units under random five-fold",
 f"cross-validation, but {rmse_sc:.2f} [{ci_rmse[0]:.2f}, {ci_rmse[1]:.2f}] on a Bemis-Murcko scaffold",
 f"hold-out of {len(TE)} compounds sharing no scaffold with the training set, with R2 {r2_sc:.2f}. Selecting",
 f"the 10 top-ranked hold-out compounds recovered a potent fraction of {hits[0]:.2f} against a base rate of",
 f"{base:.2f}. The model therefore ranks unseen chemotypes usefully while predicting their absolute potency",
 "to little better than the measurement error, and we report it with its applicability domain, its",
 "uncertainty and the code that produced it.",
]
abstract = "\n".join(ABSTRACT_LINES)
print(abstract)
n_words = len(abstract.split())
has_n = bool(re.search(r"\b\d{3,4}\b", abstract))
has_ci = "[" in abstract
hedged = sum(abstract.lower().count(w) for w in ["therefore", "while", "little better"])
print(f"\n[{n_words} words | sample sizes present: {has_n} | uncertainty reported: {has_ci} | "
      f"bounded claims: {hedged}]")
print("rung of the claim ladder used: 2-3 ('ranks usefully', 'predicts to little better than the error')")

That abstract is deliberately unexciting, and it is the version that survives review. It contains the two numbers a referee will look for (the optimistic one and the honest one), it reports an interval, and its final sentence states both what the model does and what it does not do. An abstract claiming that the model "accurately predicts ROCK1 inhibition" would use the same experiments and would be false at rung four.

15. Large language models: disclosure, and the reference check you must run

Language models are now part of how most of this material is written and coded, and pretending otherwise helps nobody. The publishers the group submits to have converged on three rules[23][24]: a language model cannot be an author, because it cannot take responsibility; its use must be disclosed, usually in the Methods or an Acknowledgements-adjacent statement; and the authors remain fully responsible for every sentence, every number and every citation in the manuscript. Surveys of researchers show the practice is widespread and the disclosure is not[22].

The laboratory's position is practical. A language model is an acceptable tool for improving the English of a paragraph you wrote, for drafting boilerplate, for explaining an error message and for suggesting code that you then test. It is not an acceptable tool for generating results, for writing a Discussion you have not thought through, or — above all — for producing citations. The characteristic failure mode is a plausible reference: correct-looking authors, a real journal, a DOI that is either nonexistent or belongs to a different paper, at rates high enough that an automated check is now part of the group's submission routine[25].

That check is twenty lines of code. For every DOI in the bibliography, ask Crossref what the title of that DOI is, and compare it with the title in your reference list. The next cell runs it on a short bibliography into which two bad entries have been planted: one DOI that does not exist, and one real DOI attached to the wrong title.

# Reference-integrity check: query Crossref for each DOI and compare titles.
import difflib
BIB = [
    ("10.1021/ci400197w", "Modeling, informatics, and the quest for reproducibility"),
    ("10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005619", "Ten simple rules for structuring papers"),
    ("10.1038/s41592-021-01256-7", "Reproducibility standards for machine learning in the life sciences"),
    ("10.1136/bmj-2023-078378", "TRIPOD+AI statement: updated guidance for reporting clinical prediction "
                                "models that use regression or machine learning methods"),
    ("10.1021/jm300131x", "A deep learning framework for ROCK1 inhibitor design"),          # planted: wrong title
    ("10.1038/s41586-024-99999-9", "Graph neural networks predict kinase selectivity"),     # planted: no such DOI
]
FROZEN = {   # responses recorded on 2026-10-18, used when the network is unavailable
    "10.1021/ci400197w": "Modeling, Informatics, and the Quest for Reproducibility",
    "10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005619": "Ten simple rules for structuring papers",
    "10.1038/s41592-021-01256-7": "Reproducibility standards for machine learning in the life sciences",
    "10.1136/bmj-2023-078378": ("TRIPOD+AI statement: updated guidance for reporting clinical prediction "
                                "models that use regression or machine learning methods"),
    "10.1021/jm300131x": "The Experimental Uncertainty of Heterogeneous Public Ki Data",
    "10.1038/s41586-024-99999-9": None,
}

def normalise(t):
    return re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9 ]", " ", re.sub(r"<[^>]+>", "", (t or "").lower())).split()

def crossref_title(doi, timeout=12):
    with urllib.request.urlopen(f"https://api.crossref.org/works/{doi}", timeout=timeout) as r:
        return json.load(r)["message"].get("title", [None])[0]

live = True
try:
    crossref_title(BIB[0][0])
except Exception as e:
    live = False
    print(f"network unavailable ({type(e).__name__}); using the frozen responses")

rows = []
for doi, claimed in BIB:
    if live:
        try:
            found = crossref_title(doi)
        except Exception:
            found = None
    else:
        found = FROZEN[doi]
    sim = difflib.SequenceMatcher(None, " ".join(normalise(claimed)),
                                  " ".join(normalise(found))).ratio() if found else 0.0
    verdict = "DOI NOT FOUND" if found is None else ("ok" if sim >= 0.75 else "TITLE MISMATCH")
    rows.append(dict(doi=doi, similarity=round(sim, 2), verdict=verdict,
                     registered_title=(found or "-")[:52]))
check = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(f"path taken: {'live Crossref queries' if live else 'frozen fallback list'}\n")
print(check.to_string(index=False))
print(f"\nflagged {int((check['verdict'] != 'ok').sum())} of {len(check)} entries")
