                         doi  similarity        verdict                                     registered_title
           10.1021/ci400197w        1.00             ok Modeling, Informatics, and the Quest for Reproducibi
10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005619        1.00             ok              Ten simple rules for structuring papers
  10.1038/s41592-021-01256-7        1.00             ok Reproducibility standards for machine learning in th
     10.1136/bmj-2023-078378        1.00             ok TRIPOD+AI statement: updated guidance for reporting 
           10.1021/jm300131x        0.09 TITLE MISMATCH The Experimental Uncertainty of Heterogeneous Public
  10.1038/s41586-024-99999-9        0.00  DOI NOT FOUND                                                    -

flagged 2 of 6 entries

# The same result as a figure, because a submission checklist is read at a glance.
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.8, 3.0))
cols = ["#009E73" if v == "ok" else "#D55E00" for v in check["verdict"]]
ypos = np.arange(len(check))[::-1]
ax.barh(ypos, check["similarity"], color=cols, height=0.55)
ax.axvline(0.75, color="black", ls="--", lw=1.0)
ax.text(0.76, ypos.max() + 0.45, "acceptance threshold 0.75", fontsize=8)
for yy, (doi, v) in zip(ypos, zip(check["doi"], check["verdict"])):
    ax.text(0.02, yy, f"{doi}  [{v}]", va="center", fontsize=7.5,
            color="white" if v == "ok" else "black")
ax.set_yticks([]); ax.set_xlim(0, 1.25); ax.set_xlabel("title similarity to the registered record")
ax.set_title("Reference-integrity check of a six-entry bibliography")
plt.show()
print("the two planted entries are the only ones below the threshold:",
      ", ".join(check.loc[check['verdict'] != 'ok', 'doi']))

the two planted entries are the only ones below the threshold: 10.1021/jm300131x, 10.1038/s41586-024-99999-9

Figure 10. Title similarity between each bibliography entry and the record registered for its DOI. Four entries match almost exactly; the fifth is a real DOI (a 2012 paper on the experimental uncertainty of public affinity data) carrying a fabricated title, and the sixth is a DOI that was never registered. Both planted errors are caught, and neither would have been caught by reading the reference list.

The threshold of 0.75 is a choice, not a law: subtitles, non-ASCII characters and markup in the registered record depress the similarity of good entries, which is why the check flags rather than deletes. Run it before every submission; it catches errors copied from a slide deck or a colleague's manuscript as readily as those from a language model.

A worked disclosure statement, in the form the laboratory uses:

Statement on the use of generative tools

During the preparation of this work the authors used a large language model to improve the readability and the English style of several paragraphs of the Introduction and Discussion, and to draft docstrings in the analysis code. All text was subsequently reviewed and edited by the authors, every reference was verified against its registered Crossref record, and all code was tested against the unit tests in the deposited repository. The authors take full responsibility for the content of the publication.

16. Summary

The last mile is computation, not decoration. Figures, tables, the Methods paragraph, the availability statements, the checklists and even the abstract can be generated from the analysis that produced the results, and the ones that are generated stay correct when the results change.

Figures are physical objects. Draw at the final width in centimetres, set the font size once in a stylesheet, export vector with embedded fonts, and check the figure under colour-vision deficiency and in greyscale before it is submitted[1][6][8]. The remake in Section 5 changed nothing about the data and everything about what a reader can take from it.

The misleading figure is the dangerous one. A truncated axis turned a difference of about 0.15 log units — a third of the experimental noise, with a confidence interval containing zero — into a visual factor of about four, and a bar of means hid two almost completely overlapping distributions[5]. Bars start at zero; means travel with their distributions; differences are plotted against the noise floor.

Digits are claims. Round the uncertainty first, then the value; report an error in the units of the target, a rank metric, the sample size and the split; and never let a single flattering metric stand for the model's performance[2][31][32].

Checklists are cheap insurance. OECD and QMRF for QSAR[12][13], TRIPOD+AI for clinical prediction[10], MIAME and MINSEQE for omics[11], LiveCoMS for simulation[15][16]: fill in the applicable one, mark partly-met items honestly, leave the rest unscored.

Disclose the tools and verify the references. A language model is a writing and coding assistant whose use is disclosed and whose output is checked; the reference-integrity check of Section 15 is twenty lines and catches the one error that most damages a manuscript's credibility[25].

What follows this unit is the machinery that makes the claims checkable by someone else: Unit 24 turns the analysis code into a tested package, Unit 25 into a workflow that runs on a cluster, and Unit 26 into a tool a collaborator can use — each with its own form of documentation, and each pointing back at the figures and numbers assembled here.

Bridge

The evidence communicated here was built earlier in this course and in its sister courses. The exploratory figure remade in Section 5 comes from Unit 5; the experimental error floor and the data card from Unit 6; the scaffold split and the honest metric from Unit 12; the model from Unit 14; the applicability domain and the OECD discussion from Unit 17; the enrichment panel from Unit 19; the simulation reporting items from Unit 20 and the omics ones from Unit 21. In the cheminformatics course, Data curation and Validation cover the chemistry-specific reporting that referees at cheminformatics journals expect, and Classical QSAR the QMRF tradition. In the bioinformatics course, Molecular dynamics supplies the simulation protocol details that LiveCoMS asks you to report, and in the AI course Model evaluation covers the metric definitions quoted in the tables above.

17. Self-assessment

1. A journal asks for figures at 300 dpi, maximum width 8.5 cm. You drew your figure at the matplotlib default size. What exactly goes wrong, and what is the fix?

The default figure is 6.4 inches = 16.3 cm wide, so the typesetter scales it by 0.52. Every font, line width and marker shrinks by the same factor: a 9-point label arrives at about 4.4 points, below the publisher's minimum, and hairlines disappear. Enlarging the fonts afterwards changes the layout. The fix is to set figsize=(8.5/2.54, h) before drawing, choose the font size at that size, and export vector (PDF) so the dpi requirement applies only to raster panels.

2. Why is a PDF usually smaller than a 300 dpi PNG of the same scatter plot, and when is the reverse true?

A PDF stores one drawing instruction per mark, a PNG stores every pixel of the canvas. With a few thousand marks the instructions win, as measured in Section 2. The reverse is true once the number of marks approaches the number of pixels — tens of thousands of points, a dense heat map, a rendered molecular surface — which is when rasterized=True on the heavy artist, keeping the axes and text vector, is the right compromise.

3. Your supervisor says the two scaffold families in Figure 5 "clearly differ in potency". What do you answer, with numbers?

The difference of means is about 0.15 log units, its bootstrap confidence interval includes zero, Cohen's d is below 0.2, and the experimental standard deviation of a single measurement is roughly three and a half times the difference itself. The honest statement is that the two families are indistinguishable at the precision of the data; the truncated-axis bar chart created the impression of a difference by removing the zero and the spread.

4. Write the reported value for a metric of 0.73819 with a 95 % interval of [0.70, 0.78].

The half-width is about 0.04, one significant figure, two decimals; so the value is reported as 0.74 with the interval [0.70, 0.78]. Reporting 0.73819 claims five significant figures for a quantity known to two. Had the half-width been 0.012, two significant figures would be kept and the value reported as 0.738.

5. Which number belongs in the abstract: the random-split RMSE or the scaffold-split RMSE?

Both, with the claim attached to the scaffold one. Quoting only the random-split value answers a question nobody asked (how well the model interpolates among chemotypes it has already seen) and is the single most common over-claim in ligand-based modelling papers. The pair also tells the reader how much of the apparent performance was scaffold memorisation.

6. Your model is for predicting a compound's potency. Do you fill in TRIPOD+AI?

No, or only the items that generalise. TRIPOD+AI is written for prediction models whose outcome is a clinical event in people, and most of its items — participants, eligibility, subgroup fairness, calibration in clinical terms — have no referent in a QSAR study. The applicable checklist is the OECD set with a QMRF; TRIPOD+AI becomes the right one the moment the group's biomedical projects predict a patient outcome. Filling in every checklist for every paper produces long tables of "not applicable" and hides the items that matter.

7. What must a data-availability statement contain to be useful?

The identity of the source (database, release, accession or query), the location of the derived data (repository with a persistent identifier), the licence, and the checksum or row count that lets a reader confirm they have the same file. "Available from the authors on reasonable request" fails all four and is empirically equivalent to unavailable.

8. The data came from ChEMBL. What licence can your curated table carry?

CC BY-SA 3.0, the same as the source, because share-alike propagates to derivative works. The code that produced the table can still be MIT: the licence of the data and the licence of the software are separate. A trained model whose parameters encode the data is treated by the group as a derivative of the data.

9. Describe the reference-integrity check in three steps and state its two failure modes.

For each DOI in the bibliography: request https://api.crossref.org/works/<doi>, read the registered title, compare it with the cited title by string similarity, and flag entries below a threshold. It fails in two directions: false alarms, when the registered title contains markup, a subtitle or non-ASCII characters; and misses, when a reference has no DOI at all, which is the case for books, theses and some conference papers — those still require a human check.

10. What may a language model legitimately do in the preparation of a paper from this laboratory, and what must be disclosed?

It may improve the English of text the authors wrote, draft boilerplate such as availability statements and docstrings, explain errors and suggest code that is then tested. It may not generate results, write an argument the authors have not made, or supply citations. Its use is disclosed in a short statement naming what it was used for, the authors verify every reference and every number, and authorship remains with the humans who take responsibility.

11. A referee asks why your Methods state the random seed. What is the answer?

Because without it the reported numbers are a sample from a distribution the reader cannot reproduce. With the seed, the scaffold split, the bootstrap intervals and the forest are all deterministic, and any difference the reader observes indicates a difference in the environment — a different library version, a different platform — which is itself worth knowing. A seed does not make a result robust; reporting the variability across seeds does that, and the two are complementary.

12. Why does the laboratory write the figure captions before the Results section?

Because a caption forces the claim to point at visible evidence. If the caption cannot be written in two or three sentences that a reader who skipped the text would understand, the panel is not finished — and the claims that turn out to point at nothing are deleted while deleting them is still cheap. It also fixes the order of the figures, which fixes the order of the argument.

Glossary

Applicability domain
The region of chemical or feature space in which a model's predictions are considered reliable, stated explicitly and supported by evidence of degradation outside it.
Bootstrap confidence interval
Interval obtained by resampling the test cases with replacement and taking percentiles of the recomputed metric.
Caption contract
The requirement that a caption let a reader who skipped the text understand the panel, name the statistical objects shown, give the sample size, and assert nothing the panel does not show.
Constrained layout
matplotlib's layout engine that allocates space for labels, legends and colour bars so that multi-panel figures do not collide.
Data-availability statement
The sentence naming the source, location, licence and identifier of the data behind a paper.
Deuteranopia
The most common colour-vision deficiency, a reduced ability to distinguish red from green; simulated here by a linear transformation of sRGB values.
Figure ordering
The convention that figures run data, method, main result, control, application, and that panels are read left to right as an argument.
LiveCoMS best practices
Community articles specifying what a molecular-simulation paper must report: force field, water model, thermostat, time step, equilibration, replicas and correlation-aware uncertainty.
MIAME / MINSEQE
Minimum-information standards for microarray and sequencing experiments: raw data, processed data, sample annotation, design, platform and protocols, deposited with an accession.
Okabe-Ito palette
An eight-colour categorical palette that remains distinguishable under the common colour-vision deficiencies.
Perceptually uniform colour map
A sequential map (viridis, cividis, magma) whose luminance increases monotonically, so equal steps in value look like equal steps in colour and the map survives greyscale printing.
QMRF
QSAR Model Reporting Format: the structured document whose nine sections record a model against the five OECD validation principles.
rcParams / stylesheet
matplotlib's global configuration dictionary, and the file that stores it, used to fix the appearance of every figure in a manuscript in one place.
Significant figures tied to uncertainty
The convention of rounding the uncertainty to one significant figure (two if it begins with 1) and the value to the same decimal place.
TRIPOD+AI
The 2024 reporting guideline for prediction models of clinical outcomes developed with regression or machine learning.
Vector vs raster
Formats that store drawing instructions (PDF, SVG, EPS) versus pixels (PNG, TIFF); vector is resolution-independent and preferred for plots with a moderate number of marks.

Textbooks

  • Tufte ER. The Visual Display of Quantitative Information. 2nd ed. Graphics Press; 2001. - The source of the data-ink argument and of the vocabulary for discussing chartjunk.
  • VanderPlas J. Python Data Science Handbook. 2nd ed. O'Reilly; 2022 (free online). - Chapter 4 is the most efficient matplotlib reference for the operations used here.
  • Healy K. Data Visualization: A Practical Introduction. Princeton University Press; 2018 (free online). - Why a plot works, with the perceptual evidence.
  • Schimel J. Writing Science. Oxford University Press; 2012. - The narrative structure of a scientific argument, at paragraph resolution.

Online resources

  • OECD. Guidance Document on the Validation of (Quantitative) Structure-Activity Relationship [(Q)SAR] Models, ENV/JM/MONO(2007)2, and the JRC QMRF template: oecd.org.
  • ICMJE. Recommendations for the Conduct, Reporting, Editing, and Publication of Scholarly Work in Medical Journals, section on artificial intelligence-assisted technology: icmje.org/recommendations.
  • EQUATOR Network, the index of reporting guidelines including TRIPOD+AI, STARD and CONSORT: equator-network.org.
  • matplotlib user guide, "Customizing matplotlib with style sheets and rcParams": matplotlib.org.
  • Crossref REST API documentation, used by the reference-integrity check: api.crossref.org.
  • The Turing Way, chapters on research communication and open-access publishing: the-turing-way.netlify.app.
